analysis.one_liner: Ends normal trade relations with China and applies far higher tariffs to all Chinese imports.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have replaced today's low tariffs on Chinese goods with much higher Smoot-Hawley-era rates, died in committee without a single vote in 17 months.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strip China of "normal trade relations" status, which is the low-tariff treatment the U.S. gives most trading partners. Instead, imports from China would pay the much higher "Column 2" rates left over from the 1930 Smoot-Hawley tariff law, and the President could push rates even higher. The change would take effect two years after the bill became law.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. manufacturers that compete directly with Chinese imports — in steel, electronics, textiles, machinery, and similar sectors — would gain a protective wall, since Chinese goods would suddenly cost far more at the border, letting domestic producers raise their own prices or win back sales. Workers in those import-competing industries are the people the sponsor says he is defending. Domestic producers of substitute goods gain indirectly as Chinese products become more expensive.

how_it_helps.text: Withdraws normal trade relations from China, so Chinese products lose the low, nondiscriminatory tariff treatment the U.S. currently applies, effective two years after enactment.
Applies the 'Column 2' rates of the U.S. tariff schedule — the punitive rates that predate normal trade with China, often several times higher than current rates — to all products of China.
Authorizes the President to raise tariffs on Chinese goods even above those Column 2 rates, giving the executive a standing tool to escalate trade pressure without further action by Congress.

analysis.who_pays: American consumers and U.S. businesses that buy Chinese goods. Tariffs are paid at the border by importers, who historically pass most of the cost on in higher prices — so electronics, clothing, toys, furniture, tools, and industrial parts from China would all cost more. U.S. exporters would also bear costs if China retaliates, as it has done against American agriculture in past tariff fights. Importers, retailers, and ports handling Chinese goods bear the direct compliance and cost burden.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies Column 2 rates to every product of China with no carve-outs, so the price increase would hit consumer staples — clothing, electronics, household goods — not just strategically sensitive goods; importers pass tariff costs to American buyers as higher prices.

Blanket tariffs of this size historically invite retaliation from the targeted country, and U.S. exporters — particularly farmers, whose sales have been the primary target of Chinese retaliation in past trade disputes — would bear that cost.

Column 2 rates are the pre-1934 Smoot-Hawley-era rates, far above anything in force today, so the bill would be the largest single tariff increase in modern U.S. history, with economists' consensus that such costs fall mainly on domestic consumers rather than the targeted foreign producer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real protection to a narrow slice of the economy — import-competing manufacturers and their workers — but pays for it with higher prices on the everyday goods every household buys, because the bill's blanket Column 2 rates and the President's authority to raise them further apply to all Chinese products with no exceptions. It is a bet that hurting consumers broadly will revive domestic manufacturing broadly, a tradeoff most trade economists judge unfavorable. The 17-month silence in committee suggests even a Congress where both parties have favored tougher China policy was unwilling to take that bet up.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, sat there for 17 months, got shuffled to a subcommittee in the final weeks of the Congress, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Banks introduced the bill on July 17, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which has jurisdiction over tariff law.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor — a single House Republican — over its entire life.

The Ways and Means Committee never held a markup or vote; on December 17, 2024, in the closing days of the Congress, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Trade, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with no floor action ever taken.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers, importers, and retailers who buy and sell Chinese goods are better off that the bill died, since the sweeping Column 2 tariffs it proposed would have raised prices across whole categories of consumer goods. Import-competing manufacturers lost a chance at protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers and retailers who kept lower prices

for.name: Rep. Jim Banks
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip China of normal trade relations and apply Column 2 tariff rates to all Chinese goods.

for.name: 1 of 226 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: One House Republican cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.

against.name: Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill in 17 months; its only movement was a referral to a subcommittee in the Congress's final weeks.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican and its only cosponsor was a Republican; no Democrat signed on and no vote was ever taken, so the record shows one-party interest and no recorded opposition.

industries.industry: U.S. retailers and importers of Chinese goods
industries.note: Blanket Column 2 tariffs on all Chinese products would sharply raise the cost of the goods these companies import, costs they would pass on to shoppers. Their interest in blocking or softening the bill runs alongside consumers' interest in lower prices.

Tariffs several times higher than current rates would shield domestic makers of steel, machinery, electronics, and textiles from Chinese competition, letting them hold prices up or take back market share. The protection is paid for by every consumer of those goods.
A tariff wall of this size against the second-largest U.S. trading partner would likely draw Chinese retaliation, which in past trade fights has concentrated on American farm and other exports.
The bill's explicit target: Chinese products would lose low-tariff access to the U.S. market and face punitive, potentially escalating duties.
